problems.title: OSCILLATIONS OF ELASTIC BODIES
problems.statement: In this problem gravitational effects are to be neglected. Unless otherwise stated, substances are to be considered homogenous and isotropic at all times.

solution.statement: The official key prints the marks below. In i., the final frequency formula includes an extra factor $\mu$ before the inner square root compared with the preceding line; j. continues with $\mu^2$ and $T_{\mathrm{beats}}=T_{\mathrm{long}}/\mu^2$. These source expressions are retained.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
Consider an element d$x$ of the rod, placed at distance $x$ from the center of the rod. Its mass is $\mathrm{d}m = m\,\mathrm{d}x/L$ each. Let $2l$ be the length of the rod at some moment, and let $y$ be the corresponding length of the region $x$.

Since the object is homogenous at all times,

$$\frac{y}{x}=\frac{l}{L/2}$$

Let $v$ be the velocity of the two ends of the rod at some moment.

$$v=\frac{\mathrm{d}l}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}\left(2l-L\right)}{2\,\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{2l-L}{L}\right)}{\frac{2\,\mathrm{d}t}{L}}=\frac{L\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}{2\,\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{L}{2}\dot{\varepsilon}$$

The velocity of the element considered is

$$v(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{lx}{L/2}\right)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{x}{L/2}\frac{dl}{dt}=\frac{xv}{L/2}=\frac{2x}{L}\frac{L\dot{\varepsilon}}{2}=x\dot{\varepsilon}$$

The kinetic energy of the rod is

$$E_{\mathrm{kin}}=2\int_0^{L/2}\frac{dmv^2(x)}{2}=\int_0^{L/2}x^2\dot{\varepsilon}^2\frac{mdx}{L}=\frac{m\dot{\varepsilon}^2}{L}\left.\frac{x^3}{3}\right|_0^{L/2}=\frac{mL^2\dot{\varepsilon}^2}{24}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Let $S$ be the cross section of the rod, and $V$ its volume. The elementary work done by the tensile force σ$S$ equals the increase in elastic potential energy.

$$\mathrm{d}E_{\mathrm{pot}}=\mathrm{d}W=F\,\mathrm{d}(2l)=\sigma S\,\mathrm{d}(2l-L)=E\varepsilon\frac{V}{L}\mathrm{d}(2l-L)=\frac{mE}{\rho}\varepsilon\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon=\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{mE}{2\rho}\varepsilon^2\right)\Rightarrow$$

$$E_{\mathrm{pot}}=\frac{mE\varepsilon^2}{2\rho}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
$$E_{\mathrm{mech}}=E_{\mathrm{kin}}+E_{\mathrm{pot}}=\frac{mL^2\dot{\varepsilon}^2}{24}+\frac{mE\varepsilon^2}{2\rho}=\mathrm{constant}\Rightarrow\dot{E}_{\mathrm{mech}}=\frac{mL^2\dot{\varepsilon}\ddot{\varepsilon}}{12}+\frac{mE\varepsilon\dot{\varepsilon}}{\rho}=0\Rightarrow$$

$$\frac{mL^2\ddot{\varepsilon}}{12}+V\sigma=0$$

Dividing by $L$ we get:

$$m\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{12}\right)^{\cdot\cdot}=-\sigma S\Rightarrow\ddot{x}_{\mathrm{equivalent}}=\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{12}\right)^{\cdot\cdot}$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
Dividing also by $m$ we get:

$$\frac{L^2}{12}\ddot{\varepsilon}+\frac{E}{\rho}\varepsilon=0\Rightarrow\omega^2=\frac{12E}{\rho L^2}\Rightarrow T_{\mathrm{long}}=\pi L\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{3E}}$$

sections.title: e.
sections.statement:
Consider very thin spherical layers of radius $x$ and thickness d$x$. Their masses are:

$$\mathrm{d}m=m\frac{4\pi x^2\mathrm{d}x}{\frac{4\pi R^3}{3}}=\frac{3m}{R^3}x^2\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Let $r$ be the radius of the sphere and $v$ the velocity of its surface at some moment. The argument goes similarly as in section A.

$$v=R\dot{\varepsilon}\Rightarrow v(x)=x\dot{\varepsilon}\Rightarrow\mathrm{d}E_{\mathrm{kin}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}mv^2(x)}{2}=\frac{3mx^2\,\mathrm{d}x}{R^3}\frac{x^2\dot{\varepsilon}^2}{2}\Rightarrow E_{\mathrm{kin}}=\frac{3mR^2\dot{\varepsilon}^2}{10}$$

$$\mathrm{d}E_{\mathrm{pot}}=\mathrm{d}W=\sigma S\,\mathrm{d}r=\varepsilon E4\pi R^2R\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon=\frac{3EV\,\mathrm{d}\left(\varepsilon^2\right)}{2}=\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{3mE}{2\rho}\varepsilon^2\right)$$

$$E_{\mathrm{mech}}=\frac{3m}{2}\left(\frac{R^2\dot{\varepsilon}^2}{5}+\frac{E\varepsilon^2}{\rho}\right)=\mathrm{constant}$$

sections.title: f.
sections.statement: $$\dot{E}=0\Rightarrow\frac{R^2\dot{\varepsilon}\ddot{\varepsilon}}{5}+\frac{E\varepsilon\dot{\varepsilon}}{\rho}=0\Rightarrow\omega^2=\frac{5E}{\rho R^2}\Rightarrow T_{\mathrm{radial}}=2\pi R\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{5E}}$$

sections.title: g.
sections.statement: $$\begin{cases}\varepsilon_x=\dfrac{\sigma_x}{E}-\mu\dfrac{\sigma_y}{E}\\ \varepsilon_y=\dfrac{\sigma_y}{E}-\mu\dfrac{\sigma_x}{E}\end{cases}\Rightarrow\begin{cases}\sigma_x=\dfrac{E\left(\varepsilon_x+\mu\varepsilon_y\right)}{1-\mu^2}\\ \sigma_y=\dfrac{E\left(\varepsilon_y+\mu\varepsilon_x\right)}{1-\mu^2}\end{cases}$$

sections.title: h.
sections.statement: $$\begin{cases}m\ddot{x}_{\mathrm{equivalent}}=-\sigma_x\dfrac{V}{L}\\ m\ddot{y}_{\mathrm{equivalent}}=-\sigma_y\dfrac{V}{l}\end{cases}\Rightarrow\begin{cases}\dfrac{mL\ddot{\varepsilon}_x}{12}+\dfrac{E\left(\varepsilon_x+\mu\varepsilon_y\right)}{1-\mu^2}\dfrac{V}{L}=0\\ \dfrac{ml\ddot{\varepsilon}_y}{12}+\dfrac{E\left(\varepsilon_y+\mu\varepsilon_x\right)}{1-\mu^2}\dfrac{V}{l}=0\end{cases}$$

sections.title: i.
sections.statement:
By replacing the sought solutions into the system of equations we get

$$\begin{cases}-\dfrac{\omega^2AL^2}{12}+\dfrac{E\left(A+\mu B\right)}{\rho\left(1-\mu^2\right)}=0\\ -\dfrac{\omega^2Bl^2}{12}+\dfrac{E\left(B+\mu A\right)}{\rho\left(1-\mu^2\right)}=0\end{cases}$$

By dividing the two equations term by term we get a simpler one:

$$\frac{AL^2}{Bl^2}=\frac{A+\mu B}{B+\mu A}$$

Let us denote the ratio of the two amplitudes by $r$.

$$r\frac{L^2}{l^2}=\frac{r+\mu}{1+r\mu}\Rightarrow\mu L^2r^2+\left(L^2-l^2\right)r-\mu l^2=0\Rightarrow$$

$$r_{1;2}=\frac{-\left(L^2-l^2\right)\pm\sqrt{\left(L^2-l^2\right)^2+4\mu^2L^2l^2}}{2\mu L^2}$$

Returning $r$ in the second equation we get:

$$\omega^2=\frac{12E}{\rho l^2\left(1-\mu^2\right)}\left[1+\mu\frac{-\left(L^2-l^2\right)\pm\sqrt{\left(L^2-l^2\right)^2+4\mu^2L^2l^2}}{2\mu L^2}\right]\Rightarrow$$

$$\omega_{1;2}=\sqrt{\frac{6E\left[L^2+l^2\pm\mu\sqrt{\left(L^2-l^2\right)^2+\left(2\mu Ll\right)^2}\right]}{\rho L^2l^2\left(1-\mu^2\right)}}$$

sections.title: j.
sections.statement:
$$L=l\Rightarrow\omega_{1;2}=\sqrt{\frac{6E\left(2L^2\pm2\mu^2L^2\right)}{\rho L^4\left(1-\mu^2\right)}}=\sqrt{\frac{12E\left(1\pm\mu^2\right)}{\rho L^2\left(1-\mu^2\right)}}$$

$$\Delta\omega=\sqrt{\frac{12E}{\rho L^2}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\mu^2}{1-\mu^2}}-1\right)\approx\mu^2\sqrt{\frac{12E}{\rho L^2}}\Rightarrow T_{\mathrm{beats}}=\frac{T_{\mathrm{long}}}{\mu^2}$$

sections.title: k.
sections.statement:
Let $d$ be the thickness of the plate. The shear force $\tau ld$ can be decomposed into a stretching component along $L$ ($x$-axis) and a shrinking component along $l$ ($y$-axis).

$$\sigma_x=\frac{\tau ld\sin\gamma}{ld}\ ;\ \sigma_y=\frac{\tau ld\cos\gamma}{\left(L/\cos\gamma\right)d}\Rightarrow$$

$$\varepsilon_x=\frac{\tau\sin\gamma}{E}-\mu\left(-\frac{\tau l\cos^2\gamma}{LE}\right)$$

$$\varepsilon_y=-\frac{\tau l\cos^2\gamma}{LE}-\mu\frac{\tau\sin\gamma}{E}$$

But

$$\varepsilon_x=\frac{\frac{L}{\cos\gamma}-L}{L}=\frac{1-\cos\gamma}{\cos\gamma}\ ;\ \varepsilon_y=\frac{l\cos\gamma-l}{l}=-\left(1-\cos\gamma\right)\Rightarrow$$

$$\begin{cases}\dfrac{E}{\tau}\dfrac{1-\cos\gamma}{\cos\gamma}=\sin\gamma+\mu\dfrac{l}{L}\cos^2\gamma\\ \dfrac{E}{\tau}\left(1-\cos\gamma\right)=\dfrac{l}{L}\cos^2\gamma+\mu\sin\gamma\end{cases}$$

Multiplying the second equation by μ and subtracting it from the first one we get:

$$\frac{E}{\tau}\left(1-\cos\gamma\right)\left(\frac{1}{\cos\gamma}-\mu\right)=\sin\gamma\left(1-\mu^2\right)\Rightarrow\frac{E\gamma^2}{2\tau}\left(1-\mu\right)\approx\gamma\left(1-\mu^2\right)\Rightarrow\gamma=\frac{2\tau\left(1+\mu\right)}{E}$$

$$G=\frac{E}{2\left(1+\mu\right)}$$

figures.alt: Sheared plate and resolved shear-force components, with geometric lengths and angle gamma.

sections.title: l.
sections.statement:
The quantities involved in the shear deformation are absolutely analogous to those describing the longitudinal deformation.

$$T_{\mathrm{slant}}=\pi L\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{3G}}=T_{\mathrm{long}}\sqrt{2\left(1+\mu\right)}$$

sections.title: m.
sections.statement:
Consider very thin cylindrical layers of radius $x$ and thickness d$x$. When the cylinder is twisting, each one of them is subject to a very small shear.

$$T_{\mathrm{twist}}=\pi L\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{3G}}$$

sections.title: n.
sections.statement:
Let α be a very small angle with witch one cap of the cylinder rotates with respect to the other. Then the slanting angle of a cylindrical layer is:

$$x\alpha=L\gamma\Rightarrow\gamma=\frac{x}{L}\alpha$$

The corresponding shear stress is

$$\tau=G\frac{x}{L}\alpha$$

The elementary shear force acting on the cap is

$$\mathrm{d}F=\tau\,\mathrm{d}S=G\frac{x}{L}\alpha2\pi x\,\mathrm{d}x$$

The corresponding elementary torque is

$$\mathrm{d}M=\mathrm{d}F\cdot x=\frac{2\pi G\alpha x^3\mathrm{d}x}{L}$$

$$M=\frac{2\pi G\alpha}{L}\int_0^R x^3\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{2\pi GR^4\alpha}{4L}\Rightarrow C=\frac{\pi GR^4}{2L}=\frac{\pi ER^4}{4L\left(1+\mu\right)}$$

parts.label: a.
parts.statement:
Consider an element dx of the rod, placed at distance x from the center of the rod. Its mass is dm = m dx/L each. Let 2l be the length of the rod at some moment, and let y be the corresponding length of the region x.

Since the object is homogenous at all times,



$$
\frac yx=\frac l{L/2}.
$$



Let v be the velocity of the two ends of the rod at some moment.



$$
v=\frac{dl}{dt}=\frac{d(2l-L)}{2dt}=\frac{L\,d\left((2l-L)/L\right)}{2dt}=\frac L2\frac{d\varepsilon}{dt}=\frac L2\dot\varepsilon.
$$



The velocity of the element considered is



$$
v(x)=\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{d\left(lx/(L/2)\right)}{dt}=\frac{x}{L/2}\frac{dl}{dt}=\frac{xv}{L/2}=\frac{2x}{L}\frac{L\dot\varepsilon}{2}=x\dot\varepsilon.
$$



The kinetic energy of the rod is



$$
E_{\mathrm{kin}}=2\int_0^{L/2}\frac{dm\,v^2(x)}2=\int_0^{L/2}x^2\dot\varepsilon^2\frac{m\,dx}{L}=\frac{m\dot\varepsilon^2}{L}\left.\frac{x^3}3\right|_0^{L/2}=\frac{mL^2\dot\varepsilon^2}{24}.
$$

parts.label: b.
parts.statement:
Let S be the cross section of the rod, and V its volume. The elementary work done by the tensile force σS equals the increase in elastic potential energy.



$$
dE_{\mathrm{pot}}=dW=F\,d(2l)=\sigma S\,d(2l-L)=E\varepsilon\frac VL\,d(2l-L)=\frac{mE}{\rho}\varepsilon\,d\varepsilon=d\left(\frac{mE}{2\rho}\varepsilon^2\right).
$$





$$
E_{\mathrm{pot}}=\frac{mE\varepsilon^2}{2\rho}.
$$

parts.label: c.
parts.statement:
$$
E_{\mathrm{mech}}=E_{\mathrm{kin}}+E_{\mathrm{pot}}=\frac{mL^2\dot\varepsilon^2}{24}+\frac{mE\varepsilon^2}{2\rho}=\mathrm{constant}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dot E_{\mathrm{mech}}=\frac{mL^2\ddot\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon}{12}+\frac{mE\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon}{\rho}=0.
$$





$$
\frac{mL^2\ddot\varepsilon}{12}+V\sigma=0.
$$



Dividing by L we get:



$$
m\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{12}\right)^{\cdot\cdot}=-\sigma S\quad\Rightarrow\quad \ddot x_{\mathrm{equivalent}}=\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{12}\right)^{\cdot\cdot}.
$$

parts.label: d.
parts.statement:
Dividing also by m we get:



$$
\frac{L^2}{12}\ddot\varepsilon+\frac E\rho\varepsilon=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\omega^2=\frac{12E}{\rho L^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{\mathrm{long}}=\pi L\sqrt{\frac\rho{3E}}.
$$

parts.label: e.
parts.statement:
Consider very thin spherical layers of radius x and thickness dx. Their masses are:



$$
dm=m\frac{4\pi x^2\,dx}{4\pi R^3/3}=\frac{3m}{R^3}x^2\,dx.
$$



Let r be the radius of the sphere and v the velocity of its surface at some moment. The argument goes similarly as in section A.



$$
v=R\dot\varepsilon\quad\Rightarrow\quad v(x)=x\dot\varepsilon\quad\Rightarrow\quad dE_{\mathrm{kin}}=\frac{dm\,v^2(x)}2=\frac{3mx^2\,dx}{R^3}\frac{x^2\dot\varepsilon^2}2\quad\Rightarrow\quad E_{\mathrm{kin}}=\frac{3mR^2\dot\varepsilon^2}{10}.
$$





$$
dE_{\mathrm{pot}}=dW=\sigma S\,dr=\varepsilon E\,4\pi R^2 R\,d\varepsilon=\frac{3EV\,d(\varepsilon^2)}2=d\left(\frac{3mE}{2\rho}\varepsilon^2\right).
$$





$$
E_{\mathrm{mech}}=\frac{3m}2\left(\frac{R^2\dot\varepsilon^2}5+\frac{E\varepsilon^2}\rho\right)=\mathrm{constant}.
$$

parts.label: f.
parts.statement:
$$
\dot E=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{R^2\ddot\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon}5+\frac{E\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon}\rho=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\omega^2=\frac{5E}{\rho R^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{\mathrm{radial}}=2\pi R\sqrt{\frac\rho{5E}}.
$$

parts.label: g.
h.
i.
parts.statement:
By replacing the sought solutions into the system of equations we get



$$
\begin{cases}-\dfrac{\omega^2AL^2}{12}+\dfrac{E(A+\mu B)}{\rho(1-\mu^2)}=0,\\-\dfrac{\omega^2Bl^2}{12}+\dfrac{E(B+\mu A)}{\rho(1-\mu^2)}=0.\end{cases}
$$



By dividing the two equations term by term we get a simpler one:



$$
\frac{AL^2}{Bl^2}=\frac{A+\mu B}{B+\mu A}.
$$



Let us denote the ratio of the two amplitudes by r.



$$
r\frac{L^2}{l^2}=\frac{r+\mu}{1+r\mu}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mu L^2r^2+(L^2-l^2)r-\mu l^2=0,
$$





$$
r_{1;2}=\frac{-(L^2-l^2)\pm\sqrt{(L^2-l^2)^2+4\mu^2L^2l^2}}{2\mu L^2}.
$$



Returning r in the second equation we get:



$$
\omega^2=\frac{12E}{\rho l^2(1-\mu^2)}\left[1+\mu\frac{-(L^2-l^2)\pm\sqrt{(L^2-l^2)^2+4\mu^2L^2l^2}}{2\mu L^2}\right]
$$





$$
\Rightarrow\quad\omega_{1;2}=\sqrt{\frac{6E\left[L^2+l^2\pm\mu\sqrt{(L^2-l^2)^2+(2\mu Ll)^2}\right]}{\rho L^2l^2(1-\mu^2)}}.
$$



Reader note: the μ immediately before the inner radical in the last expression is actually printed. It has not been cancelled or repaired here.

parts.label: j.
parts.statement:
$$
L=l\quad\Rightarrow\quad\omega_{1;2}=\sqrt{\frac{6E(2L^2\pm2\mu^2L^2)}{\rho L^4(1-\mu^2)}}=\sqrt{\frac{12E(1\pm\mu^2)}{\rho L^2(1-\mu^2)}}.
$$





$$
\Delta\omega=\sqrt{\frac{12E}{\rho L^2}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\mu^2}{1-\mu^2}}-1\right)\approx\mu^2\sqrt{\frac{12E}{\rho L^2}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad T_{\mathrm{beats}}=\frac{T_{\mathrm{long}}}{\mu^2}.
$$



These μ² terms and the beats expression are retained as printed, not replaced with a different derivation.

parts.label: k.
parts.statement:
Let d be the thickness of the plate. The shear force τld can be decomposed into a stretching component along L (x-axis) and a shrinking component along l (y-axis).



$$
\sigma_x=\frac{\tau ld\sin\gamma}{ld};\qquad\sigma_y=\frac{\tau ld\cos\gamma}{(L/\cos\gamma)d}.
$$





$$
\varepsilon_x=\frac{\tau\sin\gamma}{E}-\mu\left(-\frac{\tau l\cos^2\gamma}{LE}\right),\qquad\varepsilon_y=-\frac{\tau l\cos^2\gamma}{LE}-\mu\frac{\tau\sin\gamma}{E}.
$$



But



$$
\varepsilon_x=\frac{L/\cos\gamma-L}{L}=\frac{1-\cos\gamma}{\cos\gamma};\qquad\varepsilon_y=\frac{l\cos\gamma-l}{l}=-(1-\cos\gamma),
$$





$$
\begin{cases}\dfrac E\tau\dfrac{1-\cos\gamma}{\cos\gamma}=\sin\gamma+\mu\dfrac lL\cos^2\gamma,\\\dfrac E\tau(1-\cos\gamma)=\dfrac lL\cos^2\gamma+\mu\sin\gamma.\end{cases}
$$



Multiplying the second equation by μ and subtracting it from the first one we get:



$$
\frac E\tau(1-\cos\gamma)\left(\frac1{\cos\gamma}-\mu\right)=\sin\gamma(1-\mu^2)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{E\gamma^2}{2\tau}(1-\mu)\approx\gamma(1-\mu^2)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\gamma=\frac{2\tau(1+\mu)}E.
$$





$$
G=\frac E{2(1+\mu)}.
$$



![Native shear-force components](https://pub-43290baaaff14857b5dd59610ea438c7.r2.dev/problems/rmph-2012-th-2/alternative-archive-r1/k6-shear-components.png)

parts.label: l.
parts.statement:
The quantities involved in the shear deformation are absolutely analogous to those describing the longitudinal deformation.



$$
T_{\mathrm{slant}}=\pi L\sqrt{\frac\rho{3G}}=T_{\mathrm{long}}\sqrt{2(1+\mu)}.
$$

parts.label: m.
parts.statement:
Consider very thin cylindrical layers of radius x and thickness dx. When the cylinder is twisting, each one of them is subject to a very small shear.



$$
T_{\mathrm{twist}}=\pi L\sqrt{\frac\rho{3G}}.
$$

parts.label: n.
parts.statement:
Let α be a very small angle with witch one cap of the cylinder rotates with respect to the other. Then the slanting angle of a cylindrical layer is:



$$
x\alpha=L\gamma\quad\Rightarrow\quad\gamma=\frac xL\alpha.
$$



The corresponding shear stress is



$$
\tau=G\frac xL\alpha.
$$



The elementary shear force acting on the cap is



$$
dF=\tau\,dS=G\frac xL\alpha\,2\pi x\,dx.
$$



The corresponding elementary torque is



$$
dM=dF\cdot x=\frac{2\pi G\alpha x^3\,dx}{L}.
$$





$$
M=\frac{2\pi G\alpha}{L}\int_0^R x^3\,dx=\frac{2\pi GR^4\alpha}{4L}\quad\Rightarrow\quad C=\frac{\pi GR^4}{2L}=\frac{\pi ER^4}{4L(1+\mu)}.
$$

sections.statementAfterParts:
Source-specific printed caveat:

The actual statement and key have fourteen requests a–n. The native response form repeats T_slant in l and m, then uses n for T_twist and o for C. Both copies and the native label shift are retained below, without inventing request o or silently renumbering the statement/key. The question prints cross-contraction relations in its explanatory context; the key prints the full combined stress relations. The key’s additional μ before the mode radical, its following μ² terms and T_beats = T_long/μ² are printed native expressions, not a mathematical correction added by this reader. Material sections A–E and their requests remain within one connected whole assignment.

[Complete original question and connected response sheets](https://pub-43290baaaff14857b5dd59610ea438c7.r2.dev/%D0%A4%D0%B8%D0%B7%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B0/%D0%A1%D1%8A%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B5%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B8%D1%8F/RMPh/2012/RMPh_2012_THEO_EN.pdf#page=3). Response sheets are supplements of this same assignment.

sections.title: A.
sections.statement: Consider a very thin elastic rod, prevented from bending. The rod has length $L$, density ρ, and Young elasticity modulus $E$. The cross section of the rod is to be taken as constant. The rod is slightly stretched from both ends and then let to oscillate freely.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Write the kinetic energy of the rod at some moment in terms of its mass $m$, length $L$, and change rate of the tensile strain ε.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Write the potential elastic energy of the rod at some moment in terms of $m$, ρ, $E$, and ε.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Show that the conservation of mechanical energy for the rod leads to the characteristic differential equation for an undamped harmonic oscillation. Resorting to the analogy with a point mass $m$ acted upon by the force σ$S$ (σ being the tensile stress and $S$ being the cross section), specify the quantity that plays here the role of coordinate.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Write the expression for the period of small longitudinal oscillations of the rod in terms of $L$, ρ, and $E$.

sections.title: B.
sections.statement: Consider an elastic sphere of radius $R$, made of the same material as the rod before. Let ε be the tensile strain $\Delta R/R$. The sphere is slightly compressed uniformly and then let to oscillate freely.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Write the mechanical energy of the sphere at some moment in terms of $m$, $R$, ρ, $E$, ε and the change rate of ε.

parts.label: f.
parts.statement: Write down the expression for the period of small radial oscillations of the sphere in terms of $R$, ρ, and $E$.

sections.title: C.
sections.statement:
Consider a very thin rectangular elastic plate, prevented from bending. The plate has the linear dimensions $L$ and $l$ respectively. The thickness of the plate is to be taken as constant.

The effects of the tensile stresses $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ acting on the plate are **NOT** independent, in the sense that a stretching on one of the directions leads to a shrinking on the other direction. In the limits of Hooke's Law, this can be written as:

$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon_x&=-\mu\frac{\sigma_y}{E}\ ,\\ \varepsilon_y&=-\mu\frac{\sigma_x}{E}\end{aligned}$$

where the dimensionless factor μ (Poisson's ratio) is somewhere in the range of 0.3.

parts.label: g.
parts.statement: Express $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ in terms of $\varepsilon_x$, $\varepsilon_y$, $E$, and μ.

parts.label: h.
parts.statement: Write the system of differential equations for the movement of a point mass $m$ on two orthogonal directions, using as coordinates the equivalent found at point **c**.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
Find the possible values of ω for which the solutions of the above system are simple undamped harmonic oscillations (modes):

$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon_x&=A\sin\omega t\\ \varepsilon_y&=B\sin\omega t\end{aligned}\ .$$

Express the results in terms of $L$, $l$, ρ, $E$, and μ.

parts.label: j.
parts.statement: In general, the solution of the above system of equations is a superposition of the two modes found. For a square plate ($L = l$) and a weak Poisson ratio ($\mu^2 \ll 1$), express the beats period in terms of μ and the period $T_{\mathrm{long}}$ of longitudinal oscillations of a rod with the same length.

sections.title: D.
sections.statement:
Now, instead of being squeezed, the plate is slightly slanted along one of the dimensions, by the action of a shear stress τ, as in the diagram alongside. The shear strain is defined to be $\tan\gamma\approx\gamma$, and Hooke's Law takes the form:

$$\gamma=\frac{1}{G}\tau\ ;\ [\tau]_{\mathrm{SI}}=[G]_{\mathrm{SI}}=\mathrm{N/m^2}\ ,$$

where $G$ is the so-called *shear modulus*.

parts.label: k.
parts.statement: Express $G$ in terms of $E$ and μ.

parts.label: l.
parts.statement: Find the period of the small slanting oscillations of the plate in terms of $L$, ρ, and $G$. Express the same period in terms of μ and the period of a rod with the same length undergoing longitudinal oscillations, $T_{\mathrm{long}}$.

figures.alt: Sheared plate with applied stress tau, shear angle gamma, length L and width l.

sections.title: E.
sections.statement:
A cylinder of radius $R$ and length $L$, made of the same material as before, is slightly twisted and let to oscillate freely. The torsion strain is defined as the angle θ with which the cylinder is twisted, under the stress of a torque. Hooke's Law takes now the form:

$$\theta=\frac{1}{C}M\ ;\ [C]_{\mathrm{SI}}=[M]_{\mathrm{SI}}=\mathrm{Nm}\ ,$$

where $C$ is the so-called *elastic torsion constant*.

parts.label: m.
parts.statement: Find the period of the small twisting oscillations of the cylinder in terms of $L$, ρ, and $G$.

parts.label: n.
parts.statement: Express the elastic torsion constant in terms of $R$, $L$, $E$, and μ.
